name: Light Hyssop Violet
lede: Light Hyssop Violet is a pale, greyed violet named for the herb hyssop, recorded by Ridgway in 1912 and filed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 among ten different names for the same pale-violet block.

sections.title: One block, ten names
sections.body:
Our data traces the name to hyssop, the aromatic herb, rather than a pigment or a place [1]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas plots it on plate XXXVI at hue 59″, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the same area as block 210, "light violet" [1]. In LCH terms it reads as lightness 62, chroma 21, hue 305 degrees: pale, low in saturation, and blue of true violet [1].

That ISCC-NBS block is unusually crowded: our library also lists Aniline Lilac, Chalk Violet, Daybreak, Good Omen, Light Chicory Blue, Light Lavender-Violet, Light Wistaria Violet, Minuet, Pale Wistaria Violet and Quality as other sources' names for the same small patch of color space [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[light-dull-bluish-violet]], [[dark-greyish-lavender]] and [[dark-lavender]], at 4.6, 5.3 and 5.6 ΔE [2]. The closest everyday name is [[lilac]], about 9.8 units away [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a close match covers enough of the canvas in 17, as photographed (11 by the stricter within-painting measure), which makes it rarer than 67 percent of the named colors we track [5]. It peaks in paintings from the 1800s, at 1.7 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive (8 of 8,345 paintings) [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 55 percent of its matches, by lightness rank within the canvas; varnish cannot fake that ranking [5]. The earliest match is a painting from 1854, by the painter Skovgaard, 58 years before the name's first record in 1912; that only shows the hue existed before anyone wrote it down, not that any pigment did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [5].
